title: Chapter 3 Quiz
description: Test your knowledge of semantic HTML and accessibility.

questions.question: What is the primary benefit of using semantic HTML elements like `<nav>` and `<main>`?
options: They provide built‑in accessibility roles and landmarks
They are easier to style with CSS
They work only in modern browsers
questions.explanation: Semantic elements convey meaning to assistive technologies via the accessibility tree.

questions.question: A `<div>` with an `onclick` attribute is a perfectly accessible button as long as you style it appropriately.
questions.explanation: Divs lack the button role and are not focusable by default, making them inaccessible.

questions.question: Which heading structure is correct for a page with a main title and two sub‑sections?
questions.explanation: After an `<h1>`, the next logical level is `<h2>`. Skipping or duplicating levels breaks the outline.

questions.question: What is a skip navigation link primarily used for?
options: To bypass repeated navigation and go directly to main content
questions.explanation: It allows keyboard users to skip repetitive menus and go straight to the `<main>` content.

questions.question: What does `aria-current="page"` indicate?
options: The element represents the current page in a navigation set
questions.explanation: It tells assistive tech which navigation link corresponds to the current location.

questions.question: The `<____>` element creates a main landmark and should be used exactly once per page.
questions.explanation: The `<main>` element represents the dominant content of the page.

questions.question: Placeholder text can be used as a substitute for a `<label>` element.
questions.explanation: Placeholder text disappears when the user types, has low contrast, and is not reliably announced by all screen readers.

questions.question: What is the recommended way to label a group of radio buttons?
options: A separate `<label>` before the first radio
questions.explanation: `<fieldset>` and `<legend>` associate the group label with each radio button for assistive tech.

questions.question: Which of the following is the best alt text for an image that is a decorative line separator?
questions.explanation: Empty alt tells screen readers to ignore the image completely.

questions.question: Why is it important to not skip heading levels (e.g., h1 to h3)?
options: It creates an illogical outline for screen reader users
It makes the page load slower
questions.explanation: Screen reader users expect a consistent hierarchy. Skipping levels can be disorienting.

questions.question: What is the purpose of the `for` attribute in a `<label>`?
options: To associate the label with a specific input's id
questions.explanation: Explicit association via `for` and `id` ensures clicks on the label focus the input.

questions.question: A `<ul>` inside a `<nav>` is redundant because screen readers ignore lists.
questions.explanation: Lists convey the structure and number of navigation items, which screen readers announce.

questions.question: Which element should contain the main heading (`<h1>`) of a page?
questions.explanation: The `<main>` element should start with the `<h1>` to identify the primary content area.

questions.question: What is the correct HTML for a data table header cell that applies to the column below it?
questions.explanation: `scope='col'` tells assistive tech that this header applies to the cells in its column.

questions.question: You have a navigation menu in both the header and footer. How can you make them distinct for screen readers?
questions.explanation: `aria-label` differentiates landmarks with the same role, e.g., 'Main navigation' and 'Footer navigation'.

questions.question: An image used as a link button must have alt text describing the image content, not the link destination.
questions.explanation: If an image is inside a link, the alt text should describe the link's purpose or destination, not the image itself.

questions.question: What does a screen reader typically announce for a `<blockquote>` element?
questions.explanation: Many screen readers announce 'quote' when entering a blockquote, signalling a quoted passage.

questions.question: Which of the following is the correct use of the `<caption>` element?
options: Inside a `<figure>` to describe an image
As the first child of a `<table>` to provide a title
As a heading for a section
questions.explanation: `<caption>` is specifically for tables and should be the first child of `<table>`.

questions.question: What is the most accessible way to create a 'Delete' action that does not navigate away from the page?
questions.explanation: `<button>` is the correct semantic element for an action that doesn't change the URL.

questions.question: Using CSS, it's acceptable to style an `<h2>` to look smaller than an `<h3>` for design purposes.
questions.explanation: Visual presentation does not affect semantics. As long as the heading levels are correct in HTML, CSS can style them differently.

questions.question: What is the role of the `aria-describedby` attribute?
options: To associate an element with a longer description
questions.explanation: `aria-describedby` points to an element that provides additional descriptive text, often used for complex images or error messages.

questions.question: A `<section>` without an accessible name (no aria-label, aria-labelledby, or title) creates what landmark?
options: Section (but not a landmark unless named)
It's not a landmark at all
questions.explanation: A `<section>` becomes a landmark only when it has an accessible name; otherwise it's generic. Contrast with `<nav>` which is always a landmark.
